references.text: The expression "the third day" connects to the time references in John 1:43, where Jesus goes to Galilee. The sequence of days in John 1 leads up to the wedding at Cana.
The third day is part of a series of time markers that begin with John's testimony in John 1:29 ("the next day") and structure the first week of Jesus' ministry.
Cana in Galilee is mentioned again in John 4:46, where Jesus performs his second sign—the healing of an official's son—also starting from Cana.
Nathanael is described as "from Cana in Galilee" in John 21:2, linking the disciple to the place of Jesus' first sign.
Jesus' mother is mentioned here without her name, just as she is referred to at the cross in John 19:25-26. John consistently uses the expression "Jesus' mother" instead of the name Mary.
The wedding motif in Hosea 2:21-22 describes God's betrothal to his people in righteousness and faithfulness. Jesus' presence at the wedding in Cana can be read in light of this covenant motif.

The image of an abundance of wine in the messianic age is found in Isaiah 25:6, where the Lord prepares a feast with aged wine for all peoples. Jesus' miracle of turning water into wine points to this eschatological fulfillment.

An abundance of wine as a sign of God's blessing in the coming age is a theme in Amos 9:13-14, where the mountains will drip with new wine. Jesus' wine miracle at Cana suggests that this time is beginning to break in.

The expression "the third day" resonates with the creation account. In Genesis 1:31, the work of creation is completed. Several rabbinic traditions link the third day to blessing, and weddings were traditionally held on Tuesdays (the third day).
